summary:
Cosmic Tales is an interactive 3D solar system that makes NASA’s abandoned and retired space hardware easy and fun to learn about. Students fly through space, zoom into realistic Moon and Mars models, and click rovers, landers and deep-space probes to reveal a “Cosmic Card” with a photo and key facts: launch date, launch site, purpose, destination and when it was abandoned. A “Next” button opens a YouTube-style timeline where users drag through major events like launch, arrival, discoveries, failure and abandonment, each with its own images and natural narrated voice. Search, filters and ambient space sound keep exploring simple.

It addresses the challenge by turning dry mission records into a story-driven, game-like experience for school-age learners, with short facts first and details on demand. It matters because these machines hold decades of science and lessons about exploration, yet they’re easily forgotten. All information comes from the provided NASA data, and AI tools were used in development.
details:
What it does

Cosmic Tales is a browser-based, animated 3D solar system that tells the story of NASA’s abandoned and retired hardware on the Moon, Mars and in deep space. Users fly through the solar system and explore realistic Moon and Mars models. Filters for Moon, Mars and Deep Space zoom the camera to the right place and show the machines there. Clicking a rover, lander or probe opens its “Cosmic Card”, an ID-style card with a real photo and short facts: machine name, launch date, launch site, purpose, destination and the year it was abandoned. A “Next” button opens a YouTube-style timeline at the bottom of the screen. Users drag through the major events of that machine’s life: launch, arrival, discoveries, failure and abandonment. Each event shows only its own details and an image, and it can be read aloud with natural narration with play, pause and resume. Landing-site names appear when users zoom into a planet. A search bar lets them jump straight to any machine, and an ambient space sound can be muted or played.

Benefits and intended impact

Most mission information is dense and written for experts. Cosmic Tales puts short facts first and lets learners go deeper only when they want to, so students and space enthusiasts can explore at their own pace. Following a machine’s story through a timeline teaches what it was built to do, what it discovered and why its mission ended. We want these machines, and the science they made possible, to be remembered, and to spark curiosity about space in school-age learners.

Tools and technologies

The app is built with JavaScript and Vite and runs entirely in the browser, using 3D rendering for the solar system. We used realistic 3D models of the Sun, Earth, Moon and Mars, and built the outer planets procedurally so the app stays light. All machine information, dates, locations and images come from the provided NASA data. Nothing is invented. Narration was pre-recorded with the open-source Kokoro voice model, so it sounds the same on every device and starts quickly without a live server. Throughout development we used AI coding tools. All external models, audio, libraries and data sources are credited in the Sources section of the app and in our submission.

Creativity

Rather than building another information page, we turned mission records into a game-like journey. The Cosmic Card gives each machine an identity, and the timeline lets users scrub through its life like a video. Combining a navigable 3D solar system with storytelling, narration and landing-site labels makes learning feel like exploring.

Factors we considered

We designed for school-age users, with a clean interface, short text and simple controls. We balanced realism with performance by compressing large 3D models, loading heavy assets only when needed and pre-recording audio, so the site works on ordinary laptops and phones. We kept every fact traceable to the supplied NASA data, and we reported gaps in the data instead of filling them in. We also made the design easy to extend, so new machines, events and features can be added without rebuilding the app.
